title: SHAPING FARM WORKERS’ POLITICAL TRUST: THE MODERATING ROLE OF MISINFORMATION EXPOSURE
screen_reason: A regression study of political trust, but Table 1 reports the full weighted frequency distribution of a perceived-misinformation item (“online communication channels expose people to misinformation”, 0–10) across 1,016 farm workers, i.e. verbatim shares of respondents with a denominator. That is a perceived-amount-of-misinformation-in-the-environment measure, which the protocol counts as RECALL. Included, but the only R8-legal values are single scale points, so the row is weak (see notes).

estimates.country: 19 European countries (Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Estonia, Finland, France, Greece, Croatia, Hungary, Switzerland, Iceland, Italy, Lithuania, Montenegro, Northern Macedonia, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia)
estimates.platform: European Social Survey face-to-face interviews; the item refers to online communication channels
estimates.date: 2020 European Social Survey round (fieldwork dates not otherwise specified in the text)
estimates.measure_type: % of farm workers choosing the top point of the 0–10 scale (10 = “Completely”) for the opinion that online communication channels expose people to misinformation
estimates.denominator: 1,016 farm workers (respondents in NACE “Crop and animal production, hunting and related service activities”) from 19 European countries in the 2020 European Social Survey, post-stratification weighted to the EU age structure of farmers
estimates.definition: Respondent rated the statement that online communication channels expose people to misinformation at 10 on a scale where 0 = “Not at all” and 10 = “Completely”
estimates.misinfo_def: None given; the paper uses “misinformation” throughout without defining it, and the item wording is simply that “online communication channels expose people to misinformation”.
estimates.page_loc: Table 1 “Characteristics of variables (weighted, N = 1,016)”, pp. 183–184, row “Online communication channels expose people to misinformation (E4)”; the quoted span is the second half of that table row, whose full distribution reads 0 (1,8 %), 1 (0.6 %), 2 (2.6 %), 3 (3.6 %), 4 (5.1 %), 5 (14.5 %), 6 (10.4 %), 7 (14.9 %), 8 (18.5 %), 9 (13.9 %), 10 (14.1), Mean = 6.9
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own 0–10 rating; no external classification of any content, no reliability statistic for this single item
estimates.moderator_quote: Workers' opinion that online communication channels expose people to misinformation was rated on a scale from 0 = "Not at all" to 10 = "Completely".
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR, read before pooling. Three problems. (1) The item is a third-person opinion about whether online channels expose PEOPLE to misinformation, not the respondent's own recalled exposure; it sits at the edge of the “perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment” rule. (2) No threshold share and no “share reporting any” is stated verbatim; the only R8-legal values are single scale points, so this row uses the top point (10 = “Completely”, 14.1%). Any 6+ / 7+ / “above the midpoint” figure would be a cross-category sum, and 100 − 1.8 would be a complement, both forbidden by R8. The full distribution is copied into value_raw so an adjudicator can decide. (3) The reported mean is 6.9 (SD 2.34) on 0–10, i.e. the sample leans strongly toward “completely”, but a mean is not a share. classification_level coded mixed because the item names no content, source or claim to classify. Sample is occupational (farm workers), not general public.

missed_or_uncertain: Nothing else in the paper measures misinformation quantitatively. Table 2 (correlations), Table 3 (non-linearity tests), Table 4 (hierarchical regressions, including the interaction terms E3*E4 β = 0.106 p < 0.001, E4*E5 β = −0.112 p < 0.001, E4*E6 β = 0.095 p < 0.001) and Table 5 (diagnostics) report associations between the misinformation-perception item and political trust, not prevalence, so no rows. The other Table 1 distributions (interest in politics, internet use, minutes spent on political news, frequency of social contacts, association membership, demographics) are not misinformation measures. Considered and rejected: forming a “share who see online channels as exposing people to misinformation” by summing scale points 6–10 or by taking 100 − 1.8%, both barred by R8.

rob.design: Secondary analysis of the 2020 European Social Survey, an academic-led face-to-face probability survey; respondents restricted to those working in NACE “Crop and animal production, hunting and related service activities” across 19 European countries. Listwise-complete analytic sample of 1,016 farm workers (refusals, don't-knows and non-responses dropped; the number dropped is not reported, and no response rate is given). Post-stratification weights applied because the age distribution is badly skewed against the EU agricultural labour force (50.3% of the sample is 64+ against 9.0% in the EU-28 Labour Force Survey). Political trust index Cronbach's alpha = 0.903, McDonald's omega = 0.900; the misinformation item is a single ESS item with no reliability statistic and no definition of misinformation. Analysis is hierarchical multiple regression with VIF diagnostics; no coding of any content is involved.
